set_title: Myo- names: muscle vs nerve-muscle junction diseases
stem: A 28-year-old woman has had drooping eyelids and double vision that worsen through the day and improve after rest. By evening she has trouble chewing and holding her head up. Her pupils and reflexes are normal. Her arm weakness worsens when she holds her arms out for 2 minutes. CT of the chest shows an anterior mediastinal mass.
oneliner: 28F + ptosis and diplopia worse by evening, better with rest + normal reflexes + anterior mediastinal mass → ?

whyNot.B: Duchenne affects boys with calf pseudohypertrophy; she is **28 with fatigable ocular weakness**
whyNot.C: Lambert-Eaton improves with use and lowers reflexes; hers **worsens with use, reflexes normal**
whyNot.D: Rhabdomyolysis causes painful breakdown with dark urine; she has **fatigable ptosis**
whyNot.E: Myotonic dystrophy cannot relax muscles; she has **fatigable weakness and ptosis**

why: Severe muscle weakness: antibodies block acetylcholine receptors. **Weakness worse with use, ocular onset and a thymic mass** is myasthenia gravis.

head: Means
One clue
rows: **Dipstick blood, no RBCs; CK very high**

idea.rule: Weakness worse with use, ocular first = myasthenia gravis.

set_title: Myo- names: muscle vs nerve-muscle junction diseases
stem: A 62-year-old man who has smoked for 40 years has had 2 months of leg weakness and trouble rising from a chair, with dry mouth and erectile dysfunction. His reflexes are reduced. Strength in his thighs improves after he squeezes repeatedly for 10 seconds. A chest x-ray shows a central lung mass.
oneliner: 62M smoker + proximal leg weakness better after repeated effort + dry mouth, low reflexes + lung mass → ?

whyNot.A: Myasthenia worsens with use; his **improves with effort, dry mouth**
whyNot.B: Becker begins in youth; he has **dry mouth and a lung mass**
whyNot.C: Cerebellar degeneration causes ataxia; his weakness **improves with repeated effort**
whyNot.E: Myotonic dystrophy has a delayed grip release; his strength **improves with repeated effort**

why: Presynaptic calcium channel antibodies cut acetylcholine release. **Weakness that improves with use, autonomic signs and a lung mass** is Lambert-Eaton syndrome.

head: Means
One clue
rows: **Dipstick blood, no RBCs; CK very high**

idea.rule: Weakness better with repeated use + dry mouth + smoker = Lambert-Eaton.
also: Small cell lung cancer is the usual cause

set_title: Myo- names: muscle vs nerve-muscle junction diseases
stem: A 35-year-old man has noticed that after shaking hands he cannot release his grip for several seconds. He has frontal balding, a long thin face with temporal wasting, and cataracts. His father had similar features and a pacemaker. Percussion of the thenar eminence causes a slow-relaxing contraction.
oneliner: 35M + cannot release a handshake, frontal balding, cataracts + temporal wasting + father with a pacemaker → ?

whyNot.B: Myasthenia causes fatigable weakness; he has **slow muscle relaxation**
whyNot.C: Rhabdomyolysis is acute with dark urine; his is **chronic with cataracts and balding**
whyNot.D: Duchenne starts in boys with calf enlargement; he has **delayed grip release and cataracts**
whyNot.E: Lambert-Eaton weakness improves with use; he has **delayed relaxation and cataracts**

why: Slow muscle relaxation with wasting: a CTG repeat expansion that worsens across generations. **Grip myotonia, cataracts and frontal balding** is myotonic dystrophy type 1.

head: Means
One clue
rows: **Dipstick blood, no RBCs; CK very high**

idea.rule: Cannot release grip + cataracts + frontal balding = myotonic dystrophy.

set_title: Sclerosis names: six different hardenings in brain, skin, spine, ducts and arteries
stem: A 29-year-old woman had 1 week of painful loss of vision in her right eye that recovered over a month. Now she has numbness and weakness in her legs that began 5 days ago. On looking left, her right eye does not move inward and the left eye shows nystagmus. MRI shows periventricular white-matter plaques, and CSF has oligoclonal bands.
oneliner: 29F + painful monocular vision loss, then leg numbness + internuclear ophthalmoplegia + periventricular plaques, oligoclonal bands → ?

whyNot.A: Tuberous sclerosis presents in childhood with seizures; she has **relapsing deficits at 29**
whyNot.B: ALS spares sensation and eye movements; she has **leg numbness and optic neuritis**
whyNot.C: Scleroderma hardens skin; she has **optic neuritis and white-matter plaques**
whyNot.E: Sclerosing cholangitis affects bile ducts; she has **plaques and oligoclonal bands**

why: Many CNS scars: relapsing demyelination at different sites and times. **Optic neuritis, internuclear ophthalmoplegia and oligoclonal bands** is multiple sclerosis.

head: Means
One clue
rows: **Upper plus lower motor signs, sensation normal**

idea.rule: Young woman, deficits separated in time and place = multiple sclerosis.

set_title: Sclerosis names: six different hardenings in brain, skin, spine, ducts and arteries
stem: A 55-year-old man has had 8 months of weakness in his right hand, with muscle twitching and cramps. His hand muscles are wasted and the tongue shows fasciculations. His knee reflexes are brisk and the plantar response is extensor on the right. Sensation and eye movements are normal.
oneliner: 55M + progressive hand wasting, fasciculations + brisk reflexes, Babinski + normal sensation → ?

whyNot.A: Multiple sclerosis brings sensory and visual deficits; he has **pure motor loss with fasciculations**
whyNot.C: Sclerosing cholangitis affects bile ducts; he has **wasting and fasciculations**
whyNot.D: Scleroderma tightens skin; his skin is normal with **hand wasting and brisk reflexes**
whyNot.E: Tuberous sclerosis starts in childhood with seizures; he has **adult-onset wasting**

why: Muscle wasting plus lateral cord scarring: lower and upper motor neurons both die. **Fasciculations with hyperreflexia and normal sensation** is amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.

head: Means
One clue
rows: **Upper plus lower motor signs, sensation normal**

idea.rule: Upper plus lower motor neuron signs, no sensory loss = ALS.

set_title: Cushing names: disease vs syndrome vs ulcer vs reflex (and Curling ulcer)
stem: A 45-year-old man is brought in after a head injury in a fall. He becomes drowsy 3 hours later. Blood pressure rises from 130/80 to 210/110 mm Hg, heart rate falls to 42/min, and his breathing becomes slow and irregular. The left pupil is dilated. CT shows an epidural hematoma with midline shift.
oneliner: 45M, head injury + rising BP 210/110, heart rate 42, irregular breathing + blown pupil + epidural hematoma → ?

whyNot.B: Cushing ulcer is a gastric bleed; he has **bradycardia and irregular breathing**
whyNot.C: Curling ulcer follows burns; he has **head trauma and a hematoma**
whyNot.D: Cushing disease is a hormonal tumor; he has **hypertension and bradycardia after head trauma**
whyNot.E: Ectopic ACTH is a tumor syndrome; he has **raised intracranial pressure signs**

why: Response to raised intracranial pressure: the brain raises blood pressure to keep perfusion. **Hypertension, bradycardia and irregular breathing** is the Cushing reflex.

idea.rule: High BP + low heart rate + irregular breathing = Cushing triad = raised ICP.

set_title: Poly- names: polycythemia, polymyositis, polymyalgia, polyarteritis, polycystic
stem: A 70-year-old woman has had 6 weeks of aching and morning stiffness in both shoulders and hips, lasting over an hour. She has trouble combing her hair and rising from a chair but has no true weakness on testing. Creatine kinase is normal. ESR is 90 mm/h. She improves within days of low-dose prednisone.
oneliner: 70F + shoulder and hip stiffness, worse in morning + normal strength and CK + ESR 90 + rapid prednisone response → ?

whyNot.A: Polymyositis has true proximal weakness; she has **normal strength and normal CK**
whyNot.B: Polycythemia vera has high hematocrit and itching; she has **ESR 90 and joint-girdle stiffness**
whyNot.C: Polyarteritis nodosa causes hypertension and neuropathy; she has **stiffness and a prednisone response**
whyNot.E: Polycystic ovary syndrome occurs in young women; she is **70 with shoulder stiffness**

why: Many muscles ache, from inflammation of the shoulder and hip girdle. **Morning stiffness, normal CK and high ESR in an older woman** is polymyalgia rheumatica.

head: Means
One clue
rows: **High Hct, low EPO, JAK2; itch after shower**

idea.rule: Older adult, girdle stiffness, normal CK, high ESR = polymyalgia rheumatica.

set_title: Hydr- names: hydatid vs hydatidiform vs hydrops vs hydronephrosis vs hydrocephalus
stem: A 72-year-old man has 8 months of difficulty starting to walk, with small shuffling steps, new urinary urgency with incontinence, and forgetfulness. CT shows enlarged ventricles out of proportion to sulcal atrophy. A high-volume lumbar puncture temporarily improves his gait; CSF cell count and protein are unremarkable.
oneliner: 72-year-old man, magnetic gait, incontinence, forgetfulness, large ventricles → ?

whyNot.A: A pregnancy disorder; he is a **72-year-old man with gait, bladder and memory problems**
whyNot.B: A parasitic organ cyst; his CT shows **enlarged ventricles with gait apraxia**
whyNot.C: A fetal edema disorder; he is a **72-year-old with enlarged ventricles**
whyNot.E: Dilated renal collecting system; his dilation is **in the cerebral ventricles**

why: Hydro- (water) + cephalus (head): excess CSF with normal pressure. **Wet (incontinence), wobbly (gait) and wacky (memory) with large ventricles** is classic.

head: Term
Means
One clue
rows: **Liver cyst with daughter cysts; sheep, dogs**

idea.rule: Wet, wobbly, wacky = NPH; ventricles are big out of proportion to atrophy.
also: Gait apraxia is the first sign

set_title: Von- names: von Gierke, von Hippel-Lindau, von Recklinghausen (two of them), von Willebrand
stem: A 35-year-old man has headaches and gait ataxia. MRI shows a cerebellar mass with a cyst and a mural nodule, and CT shows bilateral renal masses. His father had retinal vascular tumors and died of kidney cancer.
oneliner: 35-year-old man, cerebellar hemangioblastoma, bilateral renal masses, family history → ?

options.A: Von Gierke disease (glycogen storage type I)
options.C: Osteitis fibrosa cystica (von Recklinghausen disease of bone)

whyNot.A: Presents in infancy with fasting hypoglycemia; he has **cerebellar and renal masses**
whyNot.B: Causes cafe-au-lait spots and Lisch nodules; he has **cerebellar mass and renal masses**
whyNot.C: A bone disease of high PTH; he has **cerebellar and renal masses**
whyNot.D: A bleeding disorder; he has **cerebellar mass and bilateral renal masses**

why: Von Hippel (retina) + Lindau (cerebellum): VHL tumor suppressor loss on chromosome 3. **Cerebellar hemangioblastoma, bilateral renal masses and retinal tumors** fit.

head: Term
Means
One clue
rows: Von Gierke disease (glycogen storage type I)
Osteitis fibrosa cystica (von Recklinghausen disease of bone)
inflamed fibrous cystic bone from high PTH

idea.rule: VHL = chromosome 3; hemangioblastomas and bilateral clear cell renal carcinoma.

set_title: Chiari names: Chiari I vs Chiari II vs Budd-Chiari vs Dandy-Walker
stem: A 30-year-old woman has occipital headaches provoked by coughing. She has loss of pain and temperature sensation over both shoulders and arms with preserved vibration. MRI shows the cerebellar tonsils 8 mm below the foramen magnum and a cervical spinal cord cavity.
oneliner: 30-year-old woman, cough headache, cape-like sensory loss, low-lying cerebellar tonsils → ?
ask: Which term names the underlying malformation?

whyNot.A: Presents in newborns with myelomeningocele; she has **adult cough headache and tonsillar descent**
whyNot.B: Causes a posterior fossa cyst and absent vermis; her **cerebellar tonsils descend**
whyNot.C: Names only the cord cavity; she also has **low-lying cerebellar tonsils**
whyNot.D: Causes hepatic vein thrombosis; she has **cough headache and tonsillar descent**

why: Hans Chiari described tonsillar descent through the foramen magnum. **Adult cough headache, cape-like sensory loss and low tonsils** indicate type I with syrinx.

head: Term
Means
One clue
rows: eponym, type I: cerebellar tonsils herniate
eponym, type II: vermis and brainstem herniate
eponym: absent vermis, cystic fourth ventricle

idea.rule: Chiari I = tonsils only, adults, syrinx; Chiari II = vermis, newborn, myelomeningocele.
also: Syrinx gives cape-like pain and temperature loss

set_title: Chiari names: Chiari I vs Chiari II vs Budd-Chiari vs Dandy-Walker
stem: A newborn has a lumbosacral sac on the back, a bulging fontanelle and a rapidly enlarging head. MRI shows the cerebellar vermis and medulla displaced through the foramen magnum.
oneliner: Newborn, lumbar back sac, enlarging head, vermis and medulla below foramen magnum → ?

whyNot.A: Involves tonsils only, in adults; this newborn has a **back sac and hydrocephalus**
whyNot.B: Has absent vermis and a posterior fossa cyst; here the **vermis is displaced downward**
whyNot.D: Names only the cord cavity; this newborn has a **back sac and hindbrain herniation**
whyNot.E: Causes hepatic vein thrombosis; this newborn has a **back sac and hindbrain herniation**

why: Chiari II: the vermis and brainstem herniate with a lumbar spinal defect. **A newborn's back sac, hydrocephalus and displaced vermis** fit.

head: Term
Means
One clue
rows: eponym, type I: cerebellar tonsils herniate
eponym, type II: vermis and brainstem herniate
eponym: absent vermis, cystic fourth ventricle

idea.rule: Chiari II = myelomeningocele plus hydrocephalus; folic acid prevents the neural tube defect.

set_title: Chiari names: Chiari I vs Chiari II vs Budd-Chiari vs Dandy-Walker
stem: A 6-month-old boy has an enlarging head and delayed motor milestones. MRI shows a large posterior fossa cyst continuous with the fourth ventricle, an absent cerebellar vermis and an elevated tentorium.
oneliner: 6-month-old boy, big head, posterior fossa cyst, absent vermis, enlarged fourth ventricle → ?

whyNot.A: Low tonsils, no cyst; he has an **absent vermis and fourth ventricle cyst**
whyNot.B: Has a displaced vermis and a back sac; his **vermis is absent**
whyNot.C: A spinal cord cavity; his abnormality is **a posterior fossa cyst with absent vermis**
whyNot.E: Causes hepatic vein thrombosis; he has **hydrocephalus and absent vermis**

why: Dandy and Walker described absent vermis with a cystic fourth ventricle. **Big head, posterior fossa cyst and absent vermis** are the clues.

head: Term
Means
One clue
rows: eponym, type I: cerebellar tonsils herniate
eponym, type II: vermis and brainstem herniate
eponym: absent vermis, cystic fourth ventricle

idea.rule: Dandy-Walker = absent vermis plus cystic fourth ventricle; Chiari = displaced hindbrain.
also: Often hydrocephalus; associated with other anomalies

set_title: Surgery endings: -ectomy (cut out), -otomy (cut into), -ostomy (opening), -plasty (repair), -pexy (fix in place), -lysis (break down)
stem: A 70-year-old man has right-sided weakness and aphasia that began 90 minutes ago. Blood pressure is 160/90 mm Hg, glucose is 110 mg/dL and noncontrast head CT shows no hemorrhage. Which treatment is indicated?
oneliner: 70-year-old man, ischemic stroke 90 minutes ago, no bleed on CT → which treatment?
ask: Which term names the indicated treatment?

whyNot.A: Removes the gallbladder; his problem is **acute stroke symptoms**
whyNot.B: Cuts pyloric muscle; his problem is **aphasia and weakness**
whyNot.C: Opens the airway; his problem is **a clot in a cerebral artery**
whyNot.D: Fixes the testis in place; his problem is **acute stroke symptoms**

why: Thrombo- (clot) + -lysis (breaking down): dissolving the clot. **Ischemic stroke within 4.5 hours with no hemorrhage on CT** qualifies for tPA.

idea.rule: -lysis breaks down; tPA is for ischemic stroke within 4.5 hours.

set_title: Wernicke names: a word-meaning problem vs a thiamine emergency
stem: A 68-year-old man with atrial fibrillation has sudden trouble speaking. He talks fluently with normal rhythm, but his sentences contain invented words and make no sense. He cannot follow simple commands and seems unaware of his errors.
oneliner: 68-year-old man, fluent nonsense speech, cannot follow commands, unaware → ?

whyNot.A: Causes halting speech with intact comprehension; he is **fluent but cannot follow commands**
whyNot.B: Comprehension is intact; he **cannot follow simple commands**
whyNot.C: Causes confusion, ataxia and ophthalmoplegia with thiamine deficiency; he has **fluent nonsense speech**
whyNot.E: Causes amnesia with confabulation; he has **fluent nonsense speech and poor comprehension**

why: Wernicke area (posterior superior temporal gyrus) handles understanding words. **Fluent word salad with poor comprehension and no awareness** fits receptive aphasia.

idea.rule: Wernicke = fluent but meaningless; Broca = halting but meaningful.
also: Left superior temporal lesion; inferior MCA branch
Right upper quadrant field cut possible

set_title: Wernicke names: a word-meaning problem vs a thiamine emergency
stem: A 70-year-old woman has sudden difficulty speaking. Her speech is slow, effortful and halting with few words. She follows complex commands correctly and is frustrated by her errors. Her right arm and lower face are weak.
oneliner: 70-year-old woman, slow halting speech, understands commands, right arm weakness → ?

whyNot.A: Causes fluent nonsense with poor comprehension; she has **halting speech and good comprehension**
whyNot.C: Speech is fluent; hers is **slow and effortful**
whyNot.D: Causes ataxia, ophthalmoplegia and confusion; she has **halting speech with right arm weakness**
whyNot.E: Causes amnesia with confabulation; she has **effortful speech and arm weakness**

why: Broca area (inferior frontal gyrus) produces speech. **Nonfluent halting speech with intact comprehension and right arm weakness** fit.

idea.rule: Broca = Broken speech, comprehension intact; lesion in left inferior frontal gyrus.
also: Superior MCA branch; right face and arm weak

set_title: Wernicke names: a word-meaning problem vs a thiamine emergency
stem: A 45-year-old man with alcohol use disorder is brought in after 3 days of poor intake. He is confused, with horizontal nystagmus, bilateral lateral rectus weakness and a wide-based gait. Glucose is normal.
oneliner: 45-year-old man, alcohol use, confusion, nystagmus, ophthalmoplegia, ataxia → ?

whyNot.A: A stroke syndrome of fluent nonsense speech; he has **confusion, nystagmus and ataxia**
whyNot.B: Causes halting speech after a left frontal stroke; he has **ophthalmoplegia and ataxia**
whyNot.C: Causes poor repetition after stroke; he has **nystagmus, ataxia and confusion**
whyNot.D: Causes chronic amnesia with confabulation; he has **acute ophthalmoplegia and ataxia**

why: Wernicke described acute thiamine-deficient brain disease: the triad of confusion, ophthalmoplegia and ataxia. **Alcohol use, nystagmus, lateral rectus weakness and ataxia** fit.

idea.rule: Give thiamine before glucose; Wernicke is acute, Korsakoff is the chronic amnesia.

set_title: Wernicke names: a word-meaning problem vs a thiamine emergency
stem: A 55-year-old man with 20 years of heavy alcohol use cannot form new memories. Three weeks after admission for confusion and ataxia, he does not recall the nurses' names and describes a detailed trip he never took. He is alert and attention is intact.
oneliner: 55-year-old man, long alcohol use, anterograde amnesia, invents stories → ?

whyNot.A: A fluent stroke aphasia; he has **amnesia with invented stories and intact language**
whyNot.B: Causes halting speech; he has **memory loss with confabulation**
whyNot.D: Causes poor repetition; he has **anterograde amnesia and confabulation**
whyNot.E: An acute triad of confusion, ataxia, eye signs; his is **chronic amnesia with confabulation**

why: Korsakoff described permanent amnesia after Wernicke episodes. **Anterograde amnesia with confabulation and preserved attention** in chronic alcohol use fits.

idea.rule: Korsakoff = amnesia plus confabulation, after untreated Wernicke; mammillary bodies.
also: Damage to mammillary bodies and thalamus

set_title: Pick vs Niemann-Pick: a dementia vs a storage disease (and their storage look-alikes)
stem: A 58-year-old man has had a 2-year change in behavior: he makes crude jokes, shoplifts and eats only sweets. Memory and visuospatial testing are initially normal. MRI shows severe frontal and anterior temporal atrophy, and biopsy shows round silver-staining intraneuronal inclusions.
oneliner: 58-year-old man, shoplifting, crude jokes, normal early memory, frontal atrophy → ?

whyNot.A: A sphingomyelin storage disease of infants; he is a **58-year-old with frontal atrophy**
whyNot.B: A hexosaminidase deficiency of infants; he has **adult behavioral change**
whyNot.C: A glucocerebrosidase storage disease with bone pain; he has **behavioral change and frontal atrophy**
whyNot.D: A galactocerebrosidase infant neuropathy; he has **adult behavioral change**

why: Arnold Pick described frontotemporal dementia with round tau Pick bodies. **Early personality change, normal early memory and frontal atrophy** fit.

idea.rule: Pick disease = frontotemporal dementia with Pick bodies; Niemann-Pick is an infant storage disease.

set_title: Horner vs Homer Wright: a droopy-eye syndrome vs a tumor rosette (and other pupils and rosettes)
stem: A 55-year-old man who smokes has had right shoulder and arm pain for 2 months. His right eyelid droops, the right pupil is smaller than the left, and the right side of his face does not sweat. Chest imaging shows an apical lung mass.
oneliner: 55-year-old smoker, shoulder pain + droopy right lid + small right pupil + dry right face + apical mass → ?

whyNot.B: Argyll Robertson pupils are small on both sides; his are **one-sided with ptosis**
whyNot.C: Marcus Gunn pupil is an afferent defect without ptosis; he has **ptosis, dry face**
whyNot.D: Homer Wright rosettes are a histology finding, not **ptosis, miosis and anhidrosis**
whyNot.E: Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes are a retinoblastoma histology feature, not **one-sided ptosis and miosis**

why: Named for Johann Horner: loss of sympathetic input to the eye and face. **Ptosis, miosis and anhidrosis with an apical lung mass** (Pancoast) is Horner syndrome.

head: Term
Means
One clue
rows: **Swinging light to bad eye: both dilate**
tumor cells around fibrils, no lumen

idea.rule: Horner = sympathetic lesion; Homer Wright = rosette. Different spelling, different field.

set_title: Horner vs Homer Wright: a droopy-eye syndrome vs a tumor rosette (and other pupils and rosettes)
stem: A 28-year-old woman has had 4 days of painful loss of vision in the left eye that worsens with eye movement. When a penlight is swung from her right eye to her left, both pupils dilate instead of staying constricted.
oneliner: 28-year-old woman, painful left vision loss + pupils dilate when light swings to left eye → ?
ask: Which term names this pupil finding?

whyNot.A: Horner syndrome has ptosis, miosis and anhidrosis; she has **vision loss, swinging-light defect**
whyNot.B: Argyll Robertson pupils never react to light; hers **dilate on swinging-light test**
whyNot.C: Homer Wright rosettes are tumor histology, not a **swinging-light pupil sign**
whyNot.D: Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes are retinoblastoma histology, not a **swinging-light pupil sign**

why: Relative afferent pupillary defect: the damaged optic nerve sends a weaker light signal. **Both pupils dilate when light swings to the affected eye** in optic neuritis.

head: Term
Means
One clue
rows: **Swinging light to bad eye: both dilate**
tumor cells around fibrils, no lumen

idea.rule: Marcus Gunn = swinging-light test; the bad eye makes both pupils dilate.
also: Afferent defect: optic nerve or retina

set_title: Leuko- names: white patches, a white pupil, white cells and white matter
stem: A 40-year-old woman with multiple sclerosis has taken natalizumab for 3 years. She has 3 weeks of worsening left-sided weakness and clumsiness. MRI shows non-enhancing subcortical lesions without mass effect. CSF PCR detects JC virus.
oneliner: 40-year-old woman, MS on natalizumab 3 years + weeks of left weakness + non-enhancing lesions + CSF JC virus → ?

whyNot.A: Leukoplakia is a mucosal patch; she has **progressive weakness and brain lesions**
whyNot.B: Reversible posterior leukoencephalopathy follows hypertension; she has **JC virus in CSF**
whyNot.D: Leukemoid reaction is a high white count; she has **JC virus in CSF**
whyNot.E: Metachromatic leukodystrophy is an inherited childhood disease; she has **JC virus after natalizumab**

why: Progressive, multifocal, leuko (white matter) + encephalopathy: JC virus destroys oligodendrocytes. **Natalizumab, new weakness, non-enhancing lesions and CSF JC virus**.

head: Term
Means
One clue
rows: **White oral patch that won't scrape off**
many foci + white matter + brain disease

idea.rule: PML = JC virus in the immunosuppressed; MLD = enzyme deficiency in toddlers.

set_title: Dys- and odyno- words: swallowing vs speaking vs voice
stem: A 45-year-old woman has had a hoarse, breathy voice since a total thyroidectomy 2 days ago. She swallows normally and her speech is clear and fluent. Laryngoscopy shows the left vocal cord fixed near the midline.
oneliner: 45F, hoarse voice after thyroidectomy, normal swallowing and fluent speech, fixed left cord → ?

whyNot.A: Dysphagia is difficulty swallowing; she **swallows normally**
whyNot.B: Dysarthria is slurred articulation; her **speech is clear**
whyNot.C: Odynophagia is painful swallowing; she has **no pain on swallowing**
whyNot.E: Dysphasia is a language disorder; her **speech is fluent**

why: Phon = voice. Abnormal voice quality: **hoarseness from a fixed cord after thyroid surgery** is recurrent laryngeal nerve injury.

idea.rule: Dysphonia = voice box problem; dysarthria = articulation problem.
also: Recurrent laryngeal nerve runs near inferior thyroid artery
Fluent speech with a hoarse voice

set_title: Dys- and odyno- words: swallowing vs speaking vs voice
stem: A 62-year-old man has sudden unsteady gait and slurred, scanning speech after a cerebellar stroke. He chooses words correctly, understands questions and writes sentences normally. His voice is of normal quality and swallowing is intact.
oneliner: 62M, cerebellar stroke + slurred scanning speech, correct words, normal comprehension → ?

whyNot.B: Dysphonia is a hoarse voice; his **voice quality is normal**
whyNot.C: Odynophagia is painful swallowing; he has **intact swallowing**
whyNot.D: Dysphasia is wrong word choice; he **chooses words and writes normally**
whyNot.E: Dysphagia is difficulty swallowing; his swallowing is **intact**

why: Arthr = joint, here articulation. Muscle coordination fails: **slurred speech with normal words and comprehension** is a motor speech problem.

idea.rule: Dysarthria = slurred muscle speech; dysphasia = wrong language.

set_title: Hemangio- names: infantile, cherry, cavernous, hemangioblastoma, pyogenic granuloma
stem: A 40-year-old man with a family history of kidney cancer has headaches, vomiting and unsteady gait. MRI shows a cystic cerebellar mass with a small enhancing nodule. Hematocrit is 55% and erythropoietin is high. Retinal exam shows a red vascular lesion.
oneliner: 40M, kidney cancer in family + cerebellar cyst with nodule, high hematocrit and erythropoietin → ?

whyNot.A: Infantile hemangioma is a skin tumor in infants; his tumor is **in the cerebellum**
whyNot.C: Cavernous hemangioma is a venous malformation; he has **polycythemia and VHL features**
whyNot.D: Pyogenic granuloma is a skin papule that bleeds; his lesion is **cerebellar**
whyNot.E: Cherry hemangioma is a tiny skin papule; his mass is **cerebellar with high erythropoietin**

why: Blast = immature precursor. A vascular cerebellar tumor: **cyst with nodule, high hematocrit from erythropoietin, VHL** fit it.

idea.rule: Hemangioblastoma = cerebellum, VHL, erythropoietin; polycythemia.
also: VHL on chromosome 3p; also renal cell carcinoma

head: Term
Means
One clue
rows: **Most common benign liver tumor; don't biopsy**
**Red papules in AIDS; neutrophils on biopsy**

set_title: -blastoma names: childhood tumors of immature cells
stem: A 6-year-old boy has had 3 weeks of morning headaches, vomiting and clumsy walking. He sways when sitting and cannot walk heel to toe. MRI shows a midline cerebellar mass filling the fourth ventricle with hydrocephalus. Biopsy shows small blue cells in rosettes.
oneliner: 6M, morning headache, vomiting, truncal ataxia + midline cerebellar mass in fourth ventricle → ?

whyNot.A: Glioblastoma is an adult cerebral tumor; his is **a child's midline cerebellar mass**
whyNot.B: Craniopharyngioma is a suprasellar mass with bitemporal hemianopia; his is **in the fourth ventricle**
whyNot.C: Neuroblastoma is an adrenal tumor; his mass is **in the cerebellum**
whyNot.D: Retinoblastoma is an eye tumor; his mass is **cerebellar**

why: Medullo = medulla (inner), blast = immature. A cerebellar embryonal tumor: **child with truncal ataxia and a fourth ventricle mass** causing hydrocephalus.

idea.rule: Medulloblastoma = child, midline cerebellum, Homer Wright rosettes.
also: Most common malignant brain tumor in children

head: Term
Means
One clue
rows: **Child flank mass not crossing midline; WT1**
**Child midline cerebellar tumor; Homer Wright rosettes**

set_title: -blastoma names: childhood tumors of immature cells
stem: A 60-year-old man has had 4 weeks of headache and personality change. MRI shows a ring-enhancing frontal mass with central necrosis that crosses the corpus callosum into the other hemisphere. Biopsy shows necrosis surrounded by crowded, palisading tumor cells.
oneliner: 60M, headaches and personality change + butterfly frontal mass crossing corpus callosum, necrosis → ?

whyNot.A: Neuroblastoma is an adrenal tumor of toddlers; his is **an adult frontal mass**
whyNot.C: Nephroblastoma is a childhood kidney tumor; his is **a necrotic frontal mass**
whyNot.D: Medulloblastoma occurs in children's cerebellum; his is **a frontal butterfly mass**
whyNot.E: Retinoblastoma is a childhood eye tumor; his is **a frontal brain mass**

why: Glio = glue (astrocytes). The most aggressive astrocytoma: **butterfly frontal mass with necrosis and pseudopalisading** in an adult.

idea.rule: Glioblastoma = adult butterfly mass with necrosis; GFAP-positive.
also: Poor survival despite surgery and temozolomide

set_title: Charcot names: one neurologist, five unrelated findings
stem: A 16-year-old boy has had tripping and a high-stepping gait for 3 years. His father has the same problem. He has high arches, hammer toes, thin lower legs and weak ankle dorsiflexion. Sensation in his feet is reduced and ankle reflexes are absent.
oneliner: 16M, tripping, high-stepping gait, high arches, thin lower legs, father the same → ?

whyNot.B: Charcot triad is cholangitis; he has **high arches and thin legs**
whyNot.C: Charcot-Leyden crystals appear in asthma sputum; he has **a hereditary neuropathy**
whyNot.D: Charcot joint is destruction after neuropathy; he has **inherited weakness, not a deformed joint**
whyNot.E: Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysm is a brain vessel lesion; he has **a slow inherited foot drop**

why: Hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy: **high arches, foot drop and stork legs with family history**. PMP22 duplication is the commonest cause.

idea.rule: Charcot-Marie-Tooth = inherited neuropathy; pes cavus, foot drop.

set_title: Charcot names: one neurologist, five unrelated findings
stem: A 58-year-old man has had type 2 diabetes for 20 years with loss of sensation in both feet. His right midfoot has become swollen, warm and flattened over 3 months, and he walks on it without pain. He is afebrile. X-ray shows fragmentation and dislocation of the tarsal bones.
oneliner: 58M, 20-year diabetes + numb feet, painless swollen warm collapsed midfoot, bone fragmentation → ?

options.B: Septic arthritis of the tarsometatarsal joints

whyNot.A: Charcot-Marie-Tooth is inherited; he has **diabetic neuropathy and a destroyed joint**
whyNot.B: Septic arthritis is hot and painful with fever; his is **painless and afebrile**
whyNot.C: Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysm is a brain vessel lesion; he has **a foot joint problem**
whyNot.D: Charcot-Leyden crystals appear in asthma sputum; he has **bone destruction in the foot**

why: Loss of pain and position sense lets repeated injury destroy the joint: **a painless deformed midfoot in diabetic neuropathy**.

idea.rule: Charcot joint = painless joint destruction from neuropathy.

set_title: Charcot names: one neurologist, five unrelated findings
stem: A 65-year-old man with uncontrolled hypertension has sudden right-sided weakness and slurred speech, then vomiting and drowsiness. Blood pressure is 220/120 mm Hg. CT shows a large hemorrhage in the left putamen. There is no trauma or anticoagulant use.
oneliner: 65M, uncontrolled hypertension + sudden hemiparesis, putamen hemorrhage → vessel lesion responsible → ?
ask: Which lesion is the likely source of the bleeding?

whyNot.B: Charcot-Marie-Tooth is an inherited neuropathy; he has **acute brain bleeding**
whyNot.C: Charcot-Leyden crystals appear in asthma sputum; he has **a putamen hemorrhage**
whyNot.D: Charcot joint is a painless destroyed joint; he has **a brain bleed**
whyNot.E: Charcot triad is a bile duct infection; he has **a hypertensive brain hemorrhage**

why: Chronic hypertension weakens small penetrating arteries: **a putamen bleed in a hypertensive** is attributed to these microaneurysms.

idea.rule: Charcot-Bouchard = hypertensive microaneurysm; putamen or basal ganglia bleed.
